text: The square where the four gate streets meet. Stalls ring it on market days, round the well and the market cross.
An open arcade on stone posts, where traders keep their stalls out of the rain. The council meets in the timber hall above.
The parish church, its long nave facing east to a round apse. The west tower carries a slate spire that travellers see from the river road.
The lord's keep, a square stone tower with corner turrets, inside its own curtain wall with four round towers. Its gatehouse faces the town.
A stone wall rings the town, with a tower every few stretches and a gatehouse at each of the four gates. Torches burn at the gates until the curfew bell.
The castle ward's parish chapel, with a bellcote over its west end and a walled churchyard where the ward buries its dead.
The craft ward's chapel, small and plain, its churchyard crowded with the graves of smiths and dyers.
The stone cross on its steps marks the market's peace. Beside it stands the pillory, for those who break it.
The merchants' inn below the castle, three storeys round a lit courtyard where carts unload for the market.
A drovers' inn by the west gate, where carters stable their horses and wait for the gate to open.
Barges land wool, timber and wine at the stone quay below the bridge, and the crane lifts them into two warehouses.
A post mill on a mound above the town, turned whole into the wind. It grinds when the river runs too low for the water mill.
Downstream of the town and downwind of it, the tanners soak hides in vats of bark and lime and stretch them to dry.
The town's water mill on the River Ember, its wheel turned by a sluice off the current.
